newsitem.title: ALBANIA: King Leka leaves Albania, promising to return.
newsitem.headline: King Leka leaves Albania, promising to return.

text.p: Self-proclaimed king Leka left Albania on Saturday, promising to return and complaining that a referendum showing little support for restoration of the monarchy had been manipulated.

Leka left Tirana airport in a private plane, heading back to his South African home. Turnout at monarchist rallies in the capital dwindled after a July 3 demonstration erupted in violence and there was no crowd of well-wishers to see him off.
His posse of youthful, Kalashnikov-toting bodyguards remained behind.

"We are temporarily leaving the Fatherland in order not to give a chance to provocateurs working against the nation to use Our presence to worsen the situation in Albania," the would-be monarch said in a written declaration distributed by aides.

His departure saved him appearing in court for questioning about the death of a monarchist supporter at the July 3 rally. Originally summoned on Thursday, he failed to turn up, and was summoned again on Saturday morning.
"Very soon he will be back because the Albanian people will call him back," said royal court minister Abedin Mulosmani.
Some of his supporters expressed doubts in view of the referendum held alongside parliamentary elections which gave him only about one third support.
Diplomats said even that seemed high and the result was as much a protest against President Sali Berisha as a vote for the king.

Leka said in a statement there were not enough voting papers for the referendum. It said evidence of other violations had been registered with the electoral commission and would be sent to the constitutional court.
Election observers reported no serious problems with the vote, and Leka's supporters have so far showed little evidence.
"The King and the people face a huge fraud, the massive theft of the verdict of the people," Leka said in a statement.
Leka, 58, arrived in Albania in April during a violent rebellion sparked by the collapse of popular savings funds in which over 1,500 people have died.

He is laying claim to the throne left vacant since his father King Zog fled Albania in 1939 before Mussolini's troops invaded. He was barred from the country during the communist era that ended in 1990.
Early results of the referendum, held alongside the election on June 29, showed 66 percent opposed to restoring the monarchy.

But Leka, who at 2.04 metres (six feet eight inches) tall towers above his countrymen, has pledged to continue his fight for the throne -- backed by the Democrats crushed in the election by the reformed ex-communist Socialists.

Monarchist party chairman Guri Durollari said he was not sure the king would return but was convinced the monarchy offered the best hope for restoring order to Albania. "The people are used to some kind of authoritarian figure," he said.

Press reports on Saturday said investigations had cleared the police of provoking the king's supporters at the July 3 rally, and had found that the bullet which killed the man did not come from a police weapon.
